                4.7.1 Application: clustering of point sets
Let us illustrate Theorem 4.7.1 with an application to clustering. This follows
a similar idea to Section 4.5, but this time we will find clusters in point sets in
Rn instead of networks. Although the notion of a cluster is not strictly defined,
common sense says points in the same cluster should be closer together than
those in different ones.
  As we did for networks, we begin by building a simple probabilistic model for
point sets in Rn with two clusters:
 128                                Random Matrices

Definition 4.7.4 (Gaussian mixture model). Generate m random points in Rn
like this. Flip a fair coin; if it comes up heads, draw a point from N (µ, In ), and if it
comes up tails, from N (−µ, In ). This distribution is called the Gaussian mixture
model with means ±µ.
  Equivalently, consider a random vector
                                      X = θµ + g
where θ is a Rademacher random variable, g ∼ N (0, In ), and θ and g are inde-
pendent. Draw a sample X1 , . . . , Xm of independent random vectors identically
distributed with X. Then the sample is distributed according to the Gaussian
mixture model; see Figure 4.5 for illustration.




      Figure 4.5 m = 3000 points drawn from the Gaussian mixture model with
      means −µ and µ shown as two big black dots, for µ = (−1.6, 0).

   Given m sample points from the Gaussian mixture model, our goal is to figure
out which points belong to which cluster. To do this, we can use a variant of the
spectral clustering algorithm we introduced for networks in Section 3.2.2.
   To see why a spectral method might work here, notice that the distribution
of X is not isotropic, but rather stretched along µ (the horizontal direction in
Figure 4.5.) Thus, we can approximately find µ by computing the first principal
component of the data — the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue
of the sample covariance matrix. Next, we can project the data points onto the
principal component and classify them based on which side of the origin the lie
on. Here is the algorithm:

Spectral Clustering Algorithm
Input: points X1 , . . . , Xm in Rn
Output: a partition of the points into two clusters P
                                                  1  m        T
 1: Compute the sample covariance matrix Σm = m      i=1 Xi Xi .
 2: Compute the top eigenvector v = v1 (Σm ).
 3: Split the points Xi into two communities based on the sign of ⟨Xi , v⟩.

Since ∥·∥ψ2 is a norm (Exercise 2.42), triangle inequality gives

We only need to bound the second term. Note that for any constant random
variable a, we trivially have5 ∥a∥ψ2 ≲ |a| (Exercise 2.24(b)). Using this for a =
E X and using Jensen inequality for f (x) = |x|, we get
                        ∥E X∥ψ2 ≲ |E X| ≤ E|X| = ∥X∥L1 ≲ ∥X∥ψ2
where in the last step we used Proposition 2.6.6(ii) with p = 1. Substitute into
